segments.text: (bright music)
- Hello everyone.
I am Zach Peterson.

Welcome back to the show
floor at PCB West 2025.

I'm here with Mike
Buetow, president of PCEA.
Mike, thank you so much for being here
and taking some time outta your busy day.

I know this is a very busy
day for this conference
because of course, this is exhibition day.
So, thank you,

- Zach, I'm always happy
to do this for you.
You've always been a tremendous supporter.
Anything I can do to help.
- Absolutely, absolutely.
So, first things first, right?

This show has grown
pretty much every year,
I would say, right?

Or is that true for this
year compared to last year?

- It is true for this year
compared to last year.
I mean, if you go back to the mid '90s,
early 2000s,
things were a little bit different

because the industry especially
was so concentrated here

in California and in North
America in particular.

But, you know, it does
continue, you know, post COVID

to grow every year little
by little, you know,

kind of as the industry grows,
we're moving up with it.
- Okay, okay.
And so, just so folks are aware, PCB West
is not the only show that PCEA puts on,
there's also PCB East,

and that show has also
been growing post COVID.
- Right.
So,

the last four years we've
been in the Boston suburbs

in 2026, we'll still be
in the Boston suburbs.

However, we are moving from the
facility that we've been in,
which we've kind of outgrown.

We're moving to the DCU
Center in Worcester,
which is really a first class facility.

You know, Worcester is actually
the second largest town
in New England, north,
anything north of New York City,
it's Boston and then Worcester.

- Really.
- So,
but it's still very close to the epicenter
of all the Boston tech companies.
It's an easy drive from Connecticut,

easy drive from New York,
easy from New Hampshire.
We are teaming up, I should add,
with an organization called FPGA Horizons,
which does an FPGA show in London
and is moving to New England

and to the U.S. for
the first time with us.

And so we've really
adding a lot to the event
as a result of that.

- That's very cool getting
some embedded folks
on the game

because like a lot of
what you see around here
is, you know, mostly PCB manufacturing
and then of course EDA,

and then we've seen a bit more
with supply chain recently.

- Mm-hmm.
- And so you think

getting more into, you
know, embedded vendors
is gonna be somewhat of a trend?
- Well, think about it.
I mean, they really are kind of,

you know, there are technologies
that really do intersect,
you know, every FPGA has a board.

I do see them as being, you
know, very complimentary
to each other,
and, you know, I mean, for companies,
like, can I mention Altium here?

- Sure, yeah.
- For companies like Altium,

of course, which is doing
a lot on the embedded side,

you know, it really
does, I think, you know,
make it attractive for them.

However, for some of
the big component guys,
you know, AMD, Altera, Xilinx, right?

You know, these are companies
that are tied in with FBGA

in London, and some of
them have already signed
on to be at our show next year.
- Oh, that's great to hear.
That's great to hear.

So, that really is gonna
catapult things to the next level
for PCB East.
About time to see that too,
because, you know, when PCB East started,
it was this tiny little show,
and compared to this,
you know, this is a huge conference hall,
we've got tons of vendors in here,
and, you know, do you think the two
are really gonna be comparable?
- That's a great question.
You know, I like to think that,
each show has its market
and whereas PCB West

is sort of the bigger
of the brands, right?
You know, it's been around longer.
It's Silicon Valley is still the epicenter
of the universe for technology.
PCB East draws from over 30 states,

about 40 countries.
- Mm-hmm.

- Okay.
- Wow.
- You know, it's a lot easier
to get to from Europe.

- Sure.
- From Africa,
where we pull from,
from the Middle East, where we pull from.
So, you know, there are some benefits,
and then the time of the year, okay?

Because everyone's on
different fiscal years,
the government calendar ends now.
- Yeah.
- You know, whereas in the spring
there's different things going on,
and sometimes there's things

that people can get to there
that they can't get to here.
So, you know, we brought that show back
and have grown it for a reason.
And, you know, whereas some of the tracks

and certainly some of
the vendors are the same,

it often feels a bit different
than here for good reasons.
- Yeah, yeah, that makes a lot of sense.

So, in terms of what people
can see here at PCB West,

there's a lot of technical
sessions going on,

and you've got some
legends in the industry
that are giving some of those talks.

For folks who may not have
been to a PCB West show before,
give us your impression and an overview

of what folks can see aside
from this very excellent show
that we have here in the conference hall.

- Well, so, you know,
when you say legends,
sometimes it means old.
(Mike laughing)
- Well, I wasn't meaning to imply old,

but you know.
- That's okay.
They'll say that they're old.
- Okay, that's fair, that's fair.

- But the truth is, so
we have over 125 hours
of design and manufacturing programming.

- Yeah.
- Okay.
And you really want the best of the best,
you know, to teach here.
What I like about what's going on is that,

like I'm in my fifties, I
entered the industry in 1991,
and when I entered the industry,
I would hear back then about the graying
of the industry, okay?
Now, 34 years later,

I'm still hearing about the
graying of the industry.

So, a lot of those older
folks are teaching here,

but what I see are lots of
younger folks walking through,
and I'm not making this up,

you know, I see this text
message from one guy,

you know, he's 24, it's his
you first job outta college.

First time he's come to the
show, Rick Hartley is lit.
(Zach laughing)
- Very Gen Z.
- Right?
I mean, there's a 50 year age difference
between these two guys,

you know, and he's like,
you know, these old dudes,

you know are, well, I'm
not gonna use the words

he's using, but, you know-
- Yeah, yeah.
- Like he's into it,
but they recognize the passion, right?

- Yeah.
- They recognize
the knowledge,

I mean, the knowledge
comes through right away,
but the passion
of the older speakers
and their ability to communicate.

- Yeah.
- Which is really important.

You know, because sometimes
the concepts are basic.
Sometimes the concepts are very complex.
To be able to get that across in a way
that people at any level can understand
is a real talent.
And that's what I like

to think about when I
think about PCB West.

- Yeah, and that's why I have
been always saying to people
who ask me, you know, what's a great way
to learn PCB design?

I always tell them one of the
few things that you can do
is of course, come to the conferences,

and of course, PCB West is
always at the top of the list.
So, always gotta tell people to come here
and get access to the technical content,
even if they're just coming today
on Wednesdays for the exhibition day,
for the free technical sessions.
- Yeah.
I mean, look, the free technical sessions,

you had the CF or sorry,
the head of engineering
for Rainmaker Technology, right?
Cloud seeding company,

they're building drones
that are about 55 pounds
or this big or whatever,
sending up into the terra sphere,
operating at 3,500 RPM.
You know, they've got electrical issues.
They designed their own radar for this.
They've got their cameras, the LiDAR,
so many things going on, right?
They have to make sure that they can,
accomplish their function
without completely icing over and failing.

- Mm-hmm.
- You know,

there's so many things that
they have to accomplish in this.

You know, they're head of
engineering, you know, keynotes.
I mean, that's a 2-year-old company
accomplishing these really big objectives.
You've got
the CFO,

or sorry, the CEO of Neros,
which is a drone maker,
you know, sitting on a panel later today.

- Yeah.
- You know,
he's building 6,000 drones a month.
He wants to be the first company to build,

U.S. based company to build
a million drones a year.

And he wants to do it with
all U.S. sourced parts.
You know, I mean, you know,
where else can you find this, right?
And again, these are young guys, right?
But they're visionaries

and there's so much energy
that comes out of it.
And they're here to network.

They're here to find, you
know, folks that they can hire.
These guys are, they're moving

into 70,000 square foot
manufacturing facilities.

- Mm-hmm.
- Like, you know,
there's so much energy and passion,
you just get caught up in it.

- This is something interesting
that you're mentioning here,

because I was just
speaking about this issue

with someone else before
we started this interview.
You know, you're mentioning
that there's young folks coming in,
and it seems like finally disrupting
the way that we do things.

And, you know, not to knock
the folks with more experience
than myself and even than yourself.
But I feel like as you get older,

you get closer to retirement,
you get more conservatives,

and you kind of need that
young blood to come in
and shake up how things are done
and just try something different.
And you get enough of that happening
and eventually something will land.

And it sounds like this
is kind of the epicenter
for that in the hardware world
- To point,
one of them, I'm not gonna out 'em here,
but one of them actually said to me,
we don't do a ton of simulation.

We like to send things up there
and find out what happens.

- Okay?
- I mean,
and that's a great way, I mean, look,

that plays into how I am,
which is like, you know,

the whole move fast
break things, you know?

- Yeah.
- Mentality.
Like, we're gonna make mistakes, okay?

You know, let's make
mistakes we can live with,

but let's not have fear
of failure interrupt
that innovation cycle.

- Yeah.
- You know,

and I like that sort of
institutionalized risk taking

that I'm seeing out-
- Mm-hmm.
- Of some of these younger kids.
- Yeah, yeah.

And I mean, they've got
time to fail, you know?
They can fail early.
They're gonna be able to recover,
they're gonna be able to figure it out.
So, yeah.

I like that we're actually
getting some young blood
into this industry again.

And maybe the industry will be
de-graying over time, though.
(all laughing)

- Maybe I'll still have
hair when that happens.
- Yeah, right.
(Zach laughing)

Well, you've been doing
this for a long time,

so I think there's gonna be
plenty more time ahead of us
to see if that happens.
- Yes.
- All right.

So, for folks who are interested
in learning about PCEA,
what can they do?
Where do they need to go?

- Right, so they can start
at our website, pcea.net.

They can reach out to me
directly at mike@pcea.net.

I mean, I really would rather
people just send me an email
or call me, right?
Most of the things,
in fact, almost everything I do today,

is start with a conversation
I had with one of our members,
almost everything.
- Wow, wow, that's really interesting.

And, you know, the printed
circuit board industry,

and I guess the community
here in the U.S. is,
I mean, it's really tight knit,

you know, everybody
kind of knows everybody,
and it's amazing who you run into,
when you're on one of these show floors.

- Yeah, you know, I
don't know that I agree
that everybody knows everybody,
but I think that it is tight knit.

- Yeah, yeah.
- To that,

I mean, because I think
that it's open and inviting.

- That's true, that's true.
- And I really give a lot

of credit to our chairman
Steph Chavez for-
- Yep.
- Literally opening his arms
to, you know, anybody and everybody,
you know, he wants to bring people in.
He wants folks to join this, you know,
collaborative as he calls it,
and, you know, network with their peers,
get mentorship and help,
become friends, right?
You know, develop lasting relationships.
- Yeah.
Yeah, absolutely.
Well, we hope that everyone
that's listening will contact Mike.
Go learn about PCEA,

and of course, attend PCB
West PCB East in the future.
Mike, thank you so much for joining us
to talk about PCB West.
This has been such a successful show.

And to everyone that's out
there listening on YouTube
and make sure to hit the subscribe button,

you'll be able to keep up
with all of our episodes

from the PCB West 2025 show
floor as they come out.
We'll see you in the next video.
(bright music)

title: PCB West 2025: Electronics Industry Insights with Mike Buetow
